body:
Unless I miss something I believe that specs-wise the ImageBitmap API is supposed to be this fast GPU-GPU memory copy.   
It already supports all the CanvasImageSource and more as input, and is supported as input by all the contexts (for RTC you'd go through a VideoFrame).  

Now, I know that implementation-wise it's not always truly the fast API it's supposed to be, but I think that's more an implementation issue than a specs issue.

Yes, ideally `ImageBitmap` should be the fast-path that keeps data on the GPU.

Of note is that there are some foot-guns in `ImageBitmapOptions`. My favorite thing to hate on there is `premultiplyAlpha`, which I'm hoping to make a complete no-op in Chromium (I just need to remember the value that was specified because of quirks in WebGL's unpack state).

## ImageBitmap added to original post

> CanvasImageSource

Good catch, I forgot to mention this ImageBitmap API -- I knew it was Canvas2D and WebGL supported -- But I didn't know it was already/or going to be supported by WebGPU and generically spec'd to work on any <CANVAS>!  The only way I could reliably pull the pixels seemed to be a pixel by pixel copy; obviously WebGPU HDR is still bleeding edge (only a few months old)

So, it is definitely one of the candidates to commonalize cross-canvas transfers through (and high-speed on-GPU conversions between bitmaps and textures, often identical bit formats in this new HDR era).  

Many APIs are still problematic in various oft-overlooked line items such as lack of HDR; we need a test benchmark to show what capabilities exist and what capabilities are lost (e.g. loss of HDR, or limitations of framebuffer types).   I've begun to notice things like "Canvas X supports HDR, and canvas Y supports HDR, but don't seem to have an easy high performance method of getting pixels from Canvas X to Canvas Y while preserving colorspace format", and I'm having difficulty tracking all this so that's why I created this meta tracking item.

So ImageBitmap is likely the best-practices commonalty (except for non-canvas buffer types like VIDEO?)

## Test Suite needed?

So as part of this meta item, **one of us should start creating a test suite and/or tracking a table/chart matrix of what APIs support what framebuffers of what colorspaces; and whether or not colorspace is preserved**.  

- Need a test suite that tests all colorspace combinations (given emergence of HDR) on all canvas combinations.
- Need a published table matrix, sort of a living defacto 'caniuse' for a specific combo (it's too comprehensive to have just one terse caniuse page)

There's just so many combinations to test (all possible combinations of source canvas 'X' of colorspace 'A', destination canvas 'Y' of colorspace 'B') and I think a test suite is needed to help guide us to the Best Practices forward.  

And if multiple APIs are used other than ImageBitmap to complete the transfers (and bitmap/texture conversions) between canvas types, also to be listed in this table; As well as all the ImageBitmapOptions gotchas.

The number of combinations just shot up with the introduction of "near royal flush" WebGPU HDR in the last few months (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Safari).  (FireFox being the sole familiar-browser exception now)

(Maybe I will begin doing this, but my time is constrained so please steal this task from me -- and we can use this meta tracking entry.  But I can inform you that with the boom of TestUFO multi-canvas-type support and TestUFO compositing support I will definitely be colliding with this problem a lot more.  

## One Example Future TestUFO Use Case:

My own use case on TestUFO: One of the many goals is an example of porting my [CRT electron beam simulator shadertoy](https://github.com/blurbusters/crt-beam-simulator) to a single WebGL/WebGPU-required TestUFO page -- and be able to apply a specific TestUFO tests (such as beam simulator) as a 'filter' on top of any other TestUFO tests of any other canvas types (such as [TestUFO Ghosting](https://testufo.com/ghosting) or [TestUFO Photo](https://testufo.com/photo).   

Other filters might include spatial filters (e.g. CRT masks) but my invention is temporal for motion blur reduction (e.g. a better-than-BFI algorithm by successfully emulating CRT electron beam).  Then I would have things like splitscreens to compare two different independent TestUFO animations (in a single parent canvas).  So both serial (filters) and parallel (splitscreen) composing.

In other words, applying one or more TestUFO test's as a compositing filter on another TestUFO test, as well as compositing multiple TestUFO tests side by side (splitscreens), etc.  

The new TestUFO engine now supports any canvas type on a per-test basis, making it easier for me to port my own shadertoys into TestUFO.  To do so, it means I now have a  need for this meta tracking entry of compositing across multiple canvas types at framerate=Hz (480fps 480Hz too).   

Most TestUFO tests use only 5%-10% GPU even at 240fps 240Hz on modern desktop GPUs.  

*Related Fun Anecdote: [To fix MacBook stutters, I had to add a hacky busyloop in TestUFO settings gear icon](https://bsky.app/profile/blurbusters.com/post/3lgbxnks2mk2s), in a very [xkcd](https://xkcd.com/1172) way, to fix power management stutters on MacBooks in Safari/Chrome because 120fps animations stuttered badly despite 5% GPU on a M1 -- and I traced that to power management.  I was using so little GPU despite 120fps 120Hz or 240fps 240Hz that it was no longer framepacing perfectly to refresh cycles due to the M1 going to sleep between frames!!].  My TestUFO workaround (optional setting toggle) intentionally burns 60% of refreshtime in randomized-positions invisible GPU draw calls, to prevent power management stutters, which fully de-stutters Safari on external 240fps 240Hz monitor. [cc: @smfr].  Interestingly, a few weeks later [maybe TestUFO prodded things along], Apple 'mostly' fixed MacOS compositing the Safari stutters for 120fps 120Hz without needing this setting. But it still stutters a bit at 120Hz, and stutters very badly at 240fps 240Hz+ without the hack on MacBooks on an external monitor UNLESS my hack is enabled in TestUFO settings.*

Anyway; any slow API such as colorspace conversions, suddenly becomes a performance gating factor, can dramatically slow TestUFO by 10x-100x -- which is why I need fast GPU-GPU transfers, with high-speed canvas-agnostic cross-canvas compositing (while preserving HDR too!).  

BTW, some visual glitches can occur in the experimental tests. Safari Tech Preview 215 HDR images appear to visibly go SDR sometimes during compositing situations; e.g. when a HTML5 text undergoing SDR CSS alpha fade animation is occuring on a layer in front of a HDR image, e.g. the mouseover animations at the gregbenzphotography HDR page.    (Chrome does not glitch this).  It probably is only be at the final compositing layer at the browser engine level, not the buffer copies.

Note: TestUFO WebGPU support is being targetted as part of TestUFO 2.2 coming out late spring / early summer 2025.  It will support HDR in release Chrome 129+ (and Edge/Brave) as well as Safari Technology Preview 215+.

_EDIT: Correction made, I meant Technology Preview 215 not 125._

# World's First Web HDR Test Matrix

This is not even found on 'caniuse' (cc: @fyrd) yet. Due to the emerging flagless WebGPU HDR situation, I am refactoring TestUFO 2D animations to eventually support any canvas type for common 2D animations.  By summer my intent is all TestUFO animations can run on Canvas2D / WebGL / WebGPU (switchable in TestuFO settings), making flagless HDR easy in many browsers.

To make this easy, I want to team-up and/or donate time to creating a single webpage to check common HDR HTML elements (canvas/video/image). A quick visual check of true end-to-end HDR support (HTML to photons).  Also complicating testing is many VMs (e.g. BrowserStack, Parallels) do not suport HDR yet, although VMWARE Fusion does support HDR.

# Happy 404 Day

One time manual-test special for State of Web HDR on Windows and Mac.
Test Pass = brighter than #FFFFFF hex white supported.
Recommended Display: Any OLED or MiniLED. (LCD HDR = crap)

### Example Test Pass Of End-To-End HDR: Brighter-Than-#FFFFFF White

The background of the gregbenz page is RGB Hex #FFFFFF.  Anything that successfully shows as HDR, means the browser compositing framebuffer is already successfully matching display colorspace (usually float16x3 = 48bit framebuffer), and successfully displaying whites brighter than hex #FFFFFF white, confirming definitive end-to-end HDR support.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e53464a1-ecbf-4a95-b1c3-03ac79433f27)
Note: These are from the HDR image test page (the colors/gradients/text are AVIF HDR images).

# Added copyExternalImageToTexture()

This is a WebGPU API that, in addition to images, also supports all canvas types, and is theoretically optimized by the browser engine to be a GPU-GPU transfer, if not already.

As long as parent canvas is WebGPU, this may be a good way to composite any images and canvases (2D, WebGL, WebGPU) onto it.   Performance test will be needed to see if this is fast enough for realtime compositing (240fps 240Hz multi-canvas, where all sub-canvas are also redrawn 240fps apiece too). 

Since it's already implemented, this might actually be the Best Practice for WebGPU users; this needs to be clearly documented somewhere on the web that this is the high-speed compositing Best Practice since copyExternalImage can be any bitmap or canvas source, **just as long as the destination is WebGPU**.  

(Note: Fallback options for non-WebGPU situations will need alternate code paths, e.g. running a WebGL shadertoy as a filter on a Canvas2D).

## Browser Engine Implementor Optimization Opportunities

I write these suggestions to the browser engine implementors reading this; since copyExternalImageToTexture() may only currently be heavily-optimized for non-HDR situations.

- This is a GPU-GPU opportunity (bypass system memory), if not already done yet;
- Make sure it's optimized for HDR colorspaces (fast copy if same colorspace HDR->HDR)
- Verify your implementation support HDR, if not already done yet (Concern: some implementations may only create RGB textures = hidden conversion overheads creating compositing performance bottlenecks);
- Optimized memory-aligned textures store pixel rows mod 256 as per WebGPU spec (padded for odd-dimensioned textures)
- For widths divisible by 256, this is a full-framebuffer simple on-GPU "memcpy style" operation for identical color formats
- For widths not divisible by 256, it's a per-pixelrow simple on-GPU "memcpy style" operation for identical color formats (loop per scanline)
- Automatic & invisible, but I believe that some driver APIs on some plats optimize for sharing assets (optimizing memory if (A) readonly, (B) bitmaps/textures whenever identically binary, and (C) same-colorspace & mod-256 situation.  This may happen invisibly at driver level if you're using existing driver APIs (etc) since bitmaps are textures and vice versa on some GPU platforms internally inside the OS inside drivers.
- In other words, for matching colorspace (e.g. HDR) the on-GPU binary structure of a rec2100-pq bitmap and a rec2100-pq texture is identical from first pixel thru last pixel of the entire image -- if the horizontal width is divisible by 256 and that size limits is within that specific GPU's single-bitmap/texture size limitation and the pixel format is same (e.g. 64bit for float16 rgba channels).  It is useful to avoid unnecessary unintentional colorspace conversions: Check that it's already performing optimally on all the supported (HDR) colorspaces.

### (That said, I don't want to be dependant only on this path. But this is opportunistic optimization opportunity)

A WebGL version of TestUFO is successfully running in beta now; and it even supports engine hotswitching and basic cross-engine compositing (Canvas2D and WebGL).    

- It supports HDR Canvas2D and HDR WebGL (via experimental flag)
- The WebGL cross-composite is much slower than the WebGPU .copyExternalImageToTexture() route, so I wonder if it's going through GPU-CPU-GPU workflow (TBC). Either way, it works. WebGL and Canvas2D looks renders nigh near identical in SDR mode.

(I finally figured it out how to disable colorspace conversion, and get things looking identical in Canvas2D HDR and WebGL HDR -- that was a bit of a hoop jump.)
